title: Skala’s Jewish Community: A Town and Its People
summary: The memorial book’s many accounts make the community itself the essential starting point for understanding the lives and history it preserves.
editorialContent:

## A community on a border

The [Jewish community of Skala](/communities/skala/records/mention_fa3a33fc06ea6e2113905c16) grew up in a town shaped by its geography. Skala stood on the western bank of the Zbruch, a river that marked a political frontier for long periods. The memorial book describes a compact town centre amid rural suburbs, largely Ukrainian in population, with Polish families also living nearby. Skala’s Jews were not separate from this landscape: trade, crafts, farming and the border economy tied town and countryside together.

The book places a Jewish settlement here early, but its own historical account gives two different dates for the first documentary evidence: a census of 1560 and another of 1570, each said to record ten Jewish families. The records supplied for this article likewise note Jewish settlement from at least 1570. These references are best read as evidence of an established presence by the sixteenth century, not as proof of the community’s exact beginnings. The book’s much earlier estimates are explicitly presented as assumptions based partly on Jewish settlement in neighbouring places.

Independent context helps anchor the town’s changing political setting. Yad Vashem’s place entry identifies Skala as Skala, in the Borszczów district of Tarnopol, and records it successively under Austro-Hungarian, Polish, Soviet, German-occupied and Ukrainian rule. Its 1921 census figure is 1,555 Jews among 4,017 residents—about 39 percent of the population. That snapshot confirms a substantial Jewish presence, though it cannot tell us how every family experienced daily life. ([Yad Vashem’s Skala place entry](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/places/5440531))

## Work, institutions and neighbours

In the memorial book’s account, Skala’s Jewish residents made their living through small commerce and skilled trades. Some kept shops; others worked as tailors, shoemakers, bakers, tinsmiths, carpenters, glaziers or locksmiths. The book also recalls Jewish people working as blacksmiths, a trade it says was more commonly associated locally with Ukrainians. Market days connected Skala’s merchants to the surrounding countryside. Across the Zbruch, the frontier created a different kind of livelihood: the book remembers smugglers, known locally as “peckel-machers,” moving goods through a border zone where trade and danger were closely linked.

Community life was more than work and worship. The book remembers communal institutions, education and political activity, including a Zionist movement associated with the founding of a Hebrew school. [Chaim Roiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_d0d5cfbdb24f93a6f439a99f) is remembered as a respected teacher; the account of Skala’s Hebrew school is associated with him. [Esther Bner-Gelbert](/communities/skala/records/mention_cbfa72627043c8b78f206895) contributed a remembrance about him. These recollections preserve individual voices and institutions, though they do not provide a complete register of the town’s schools, synagogues or communal offices. The [Old Shul of Skala](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40) appears in the record graph, but the material available here does not establish its history or role in detail.

The community’s relationship with non-Jewish neighbours was neither a simple story of harmony nor one of unbroken hostility. The memorial book recalls economic interdependence and shared town life, while also describing antisemitism and political pressures. Its references to [Polish authorities and antisemitism](/communities/skala/records/mention_4c90beaa265d034bf80fecd6) belong to the book’s testimony; they should not be treated as a full account of every local relationship. Skala’s Jewish history unfolded amid changing states and competing national movements, but ordinary exchanges in workshops, markets and villages also connected its residents to their neighbours.

## Occupation and destruction

The memorial book’s destruction narrative is built from survivor testimony and a document it reproduces as having been prepared in Skala in July 1944. It says Hungarian forces entered the town on July 8, 1941, followed by German occupation. The document describes the occupation authorities’ persecution of Jews and the role of local administration and Ukrainian collaborators. It reports that on September 26–27, 1942, almost half of Skala’s Jewish population was deported to Bełżec; about 33 elderly and sick people, it says, were shot in the town. On October 22, the remaining Jews were expelled to Borszczów, where further killings followed through June 1943. These dates and numbers are the book’s account, not a census of every victim.

The record graph summarizes the community’s fate as destruction by Nazi occupiers and Ukrainian auxiliaries. That summary is consistent with the book’s account of German power and local collaboration, but the book itself also describes the changing machinery of persecution: German occupation agencies, police, forced labor, deportation and the Judenrat, the Jewish council compelled to carry out orders. The name [Judenrat](/communities/skala/records/mention_3dedc3e340b531fb3961c7d9) therefore marks an institution operating under coercion, not a community acting freely.

Yad Vashem’s place entry independently confirms Skala’s location and its large prewar Jewish population. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum adds a different kind of evidence: its biography of Schloma Wolf (Willy) Szapiro identifies him as born in Skala in 1910 and traces his life through Palestine, Austria and France, where he joined the resistance and was executed in 1944. He is not identified in the supplied records as a Skala survivor, and his story should not be merged with the book’s local testimony. It does, however, show how a person born in Skala could become part of a wider European history of migration and resistance. ([USHMM biography of Willy Szapiro](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/id-card/schloma-wolf-willy-szapiro))

## Survivors and the work of memory

The memorial book refuses to let the community end with the deportations. It names survivors including Shalom Grinberg, Abraham Trasavoutski, Moses Saltzman and Fishel Fish, and recalls people who made lives in [America](/communities/skala/records/mention_54e991425f4b1ce710d0e383) and [Israel](/communities/skala/records/mention_40a2a6ab95553834c816c2e8). The surviving record also names [Yisrael Feker](/communities/skala/records/mention_cbf3ccb0f2b8eef632008422) as a postwar grocery shopkeeper. These fragments suggest lives rebuilt in different places, but the evidence supplied here does not trace each person’s family, route or fate. They are not a complete survivor list.

The book itself arose from that scattering. Its foreword says former residents in the United States and Israel organized to gather testimony, documents and photographs; in 1960, a memorial meeting in New York formally launched the project. The editors emphasized that so many community leaders had been murdered that the survivors’ memories were among the few remaining sources. The result is both historical evidence and an act of remembrance: a record of streets, livelihoods, institutions and people, assembled by those who feared that the world they had known would otherwise vanish.

Two avenues remain especially worth pursuing: the documentary history of the [Old Shul](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40) and the lives of [the survivors’ relatives](research:Trace the families and postwar lives of Skala survivors Shalom Grinberg Abraham Trasavoutski Moses Saltzman and Fishel Fish). The memorial book preserves names and testimony; family records, survivor registries and local archives may carry those stories further.
